item.content:encoded:
政治

本周要闻 2026年10月1日

唐纳德·特朗普拒绝了伊朗提出的一项协议，该协议提议如果美国解除对伊朗港口的封锁，伊朗将在七天内重新向商业船只开放霍尔木兹海峡，并恢复核谈判。他告诉助手们，他预计将在11月中期选举后再次开始轰炸伊朗。特朗普先生表示，美国对该海峡拥有“完全控制权”，并且“大量石油”正从中通过。

最后一批美国和英国军队离开伊拉克，结束了他们自2014年以来在该国的存在。当年他们作为国际联盟的一部分被派往那里，打击圣战组织“伊斯兰国”。伊拉克总理表示，他们的撤离预示着伊拉克将转向“对其安全与稳定承担全部责任”。

一架从迪拜飞往特拉维夫的迪拜航空航班在副驾驶刺伤机长后，不到两分钟内骤降近两万英尺并发出求救信号，随后改道飞往沙特阿拉伯。以色列国防部长以色列·卡茨声称，初步证据表明这名失控飞行员意图让飞机坠毁，杀死机上所有人，并将其称为“一次未遂的圣战恐怖袭击”。乘客们制服了袭击者，使其他飞行员得以将飞机降落。以色列总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡称赞这位印度机长奋起反抗，是“真正的英雄”。

法蒂玛·扎赫拉·曼苏里被任命为摩洛哥首位女总理，此前她的自由党在最近的议会选举中赢得最多席位。国王穆罕默德六世选择了曾任马拉喀什市长的曼苏里女士，而非她的党内同事、足协主席福齐·莱克贾。

非洲首富阿利科·丹格特和肯尼亚总统威廉·鲁托在肯尼亚沿海的拉穆为一所耗资160亿美元的炼油厂奠基，他们希望这将降低东非的燃料成本和精炼产品进口费用。埃塞俄比亚总理阿比·艾哈迈德、乌干达总统约韦里·穆塞韦尼以及其他几位非洲领导人出席了仪式。丹格特先生已在祖国尼日利亚运营一家大型炼油厂。

几内亚比绍前总统乌马罗·西索科·恩巴洛在2025年11月的政变中被推翻，他表示将回国参加12月6日的总统选举。这一声明加剧了人们的怀疑，认为恩巴洛先生策划了这场政变——政变发生在他预计将败选的选举结果公布前夕。

特朗普先生与习近平的峰会没有取得重大突破，尽管中美两国确实同意各自削减对对方价值300亿美元商品的关税（不包括大豆），并表示将建立美中超级智能对话（中方称之为人工智能对话）。这将包括一个报告人工智能事件的机制。

英国军情五处情报机构警告英国学者，北京的中国通用技术研究院与中国情报机构有密切联系，并正在资助有助于中国间谍活动的研究。军情五处表示，学者们可能不知道这些联系，但敦促大学切断与该研究院的关系，并称如果不这样做，他们可能违反国家安全法。

马来西亚开始将首批5000名寻求庇护者遣返缅甸，这是它与缅甸军政府协调制定的一项计划的一部分。来自缅甸罗兴亚穆斯林群体的难民在马来西亚遭遇了一波敌意，面临被强行逐出村庄和学校的处境。据信该国约有12.6万名罗兴亚人。政府坚称遣返是自愿的，但联合国人员被禁止对他们进行筛查。目前尚不清楚首批离开的难民中是否有罗兴亚人。

在缅甸，据报道至少有50人在靠近孟加拉国边境的皎道镇的一次空袭中丧生。此次空袭是缅甸武装部队对若开军的最新攻势，若开军是一个分离主义组织，也对罗兴亚人犯下了暴行。

泰国的洪水死亡人数升至23人。曼谷在三天内遭遇了32厘米（12.6英寸）的降雨，导致其主要机场运营受阻。市中心的水位开始消退，但外围郊区预计需要更长时间排干。预计首都很快还会有更多强降雨。

乌克兰基辅的国家科学院在俄罗斯对首都的又一次空袭中被无人机击中。至少两人在科学院丧生。该科学院成立于1918年，负责协调乌克兰主要机构的研究工作。

英国反恐警方表示，在五名最初被怀疑企图袭击费尔福德空军基地的男子的货车中未发现爆炸装置。美国轰炸机从该基地起飞，执行打击伊朗军事设施的任务。在这五人被捕后，英国政府召开了紧急COBRA安全会议，但尽管官方怀疑伊朗介入，他们仍被保释，等待进一步调查。

于7月接任英国首相的安迪·伯纳姆在利物浦的工党会议上发表了重要演讲。民调支持率上升的伯纳姆先生传达了“再次充满希望”的信息，并表示他希望为十年的分裂画上句号。他承诺解决三个棘手问题：国家养老金、选举制度和欧洲，尽管这些改革被推迟到下一次大选之后，而下一次大选要到2029年才举行（伯纳姆先生确实宣布成立一个全国委员会来研究选举改革）。工党的反对者表示，他的演讲对解决英国今天面临的问题毫无帮助。

在法国，明年总统选举中领先的中右翼候选人爱德华·菲利普概述了一项养老金改革计划，拟将最低退休年龄从接近63岁提高到65岁。菲利普先生称法国相对较低的退休年龄是不可持续的，并表示如果不进行改革，就有爆发金融危机的风险。最新统计数据显示，公共债务再次上升，达到GDP的119%。法国的主权借贷成本升至2008年以来的最高水平。政府公布了2027年预算，承诺节省540亿欧元（610亿美元）。但它表示赤字将占GDP的5%，远高于欧盟3%的上限。

田纳西州200年来首位面临死刑的女性在执行注射死刑后活了下来。克里斯塔·派克于1996年被判谋杀同学罪，当时她18岁。在行刑失败后，她被转移到一家医疗机构。监狱管理局坚称遵循了适当程序，并称已为她注射了两针致命注射化学药剂。

巴西总统竞选候选人进入10月4日大选前的最后竞选阶段。左翼现任总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦对保守派挑战者弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗保持微弱领先，但在预计于10月25日举行的决选中，这一优势缩小到统计上的平局。

阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱在社交媒体上就福克兰群岛大发雷霆，并威胁说，除非一项英以石油勘探项目在两周内停止运营，否则将对该项目采取法律行动。米莱先生称该项目对阿根廷构成“明确而现实的危险”。他最近还抨击联合国未推进阿根廷对该英国领土的主权主张，称联合国“毫无用处”，充斥着“伪装成善意官僚的傲慢寄生虫”。

item.content:encoded:
Business

The world this week

Oct 1st 2026

Details emerged about Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which it has circulated among key investors. According to Reuters, revenue at the firm reportedly rose to $4.6bn last year, and it recorded a net loss of $42bn, $34bn of which was an accounting charge. It aims to spend $518bn in the near future on cloud infrastructure and other investments. Anthropic could be valued at $2trn when it lists on the stock market, which would smash the record $1.8trn valuation set by SpaceX only in June. The IPO is not expected until after America’s midterm elections in November. It counted “existential risks to humanity” among the hazards facing its business.

Sam Altman, the boss of OpenAI, said his firm’s already-delayed IPO would not take place until it had tackled concerns about the safety of its technology. OpenAI confirmed that it had withheld the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after its new model displayed high levels of deception during internal tests. It also suspended trials of other models. The firm has admitted that its agents breached dozens of systems, including some governmental ones.

Confronting worries about AI safety, Nvidia launched an Open Agent Safety Platform that allows companies to track the activities of their AI agents. Jensen Huang, the chipmaker’s boss, is less concerned about the threat from AI to humanity than his fellow tech titans, saying recently that it is up to AI companies to ensure their models are safe and under control. Meanwhile, Nvidia expanded its share buy-back programme by $150bn, taking its total buy-back plan to $235bn, the biggest-ever in corporate America.

AMD struck an agreement to acquire World Labs, a startup, in an $8.2bn deal. World Labs was co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher and professor at Stanford University, to develop spatial models that investigate how the three-dimensional physical world works for application in areas such as robotics and gaming. AMD’s acquisition is the latest instance of a chipmaker evolving its business towards the development of advanced AI frontier models.

The sell-off in bond markets continued. The yield on ten-year US Treasuries was over 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. British 30-year gilts crossed 6% and French spreads over German Bunds were back to euro-crisis levels. Donald Trump didn’t help by renewing his call for Jerome Powell to step down from the board of governors at the Federal Reserve, which revived fears about the independence of the central bank and the direction of inflation.

Shein’s first earnings report since listing on the stock market in early September disappointed investors. Adjusted net profit fell by 67%, year on year, and revenue was virtually flat. The ultra-cheap retailer’s share price plunged after it announced its results, giving it a market value of around $17bn, down from $26bn at its IPO.

The German government was reportedly seeking assurances from UniCredit, an Italian bank, about its commitments in any takeover of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-biggest lender, such as keeping its listing in Frankfurt. The government has so far resisted UniCredit’s advances on Commerzbank, but has moderated its opposition to a deal. The Italians are preparing to take control as early as January next year, according to reports, and plan a big restructuring of the bank, including ditching some international business.

Tata Trusts, the charitable group which owns 66% of Tata Sons, proposed merging the holding company with two subsidiaries to avoid a forced public listing. The proposal, led by Noel Tata, a scion of the Tata family, challenges the board’s recent decision to proceed with an IPO.

SpaceX’s Starship rocket marked a milestone by reaching orbit for the first time, despite a failure in one of its three main engines, which cut short its flying time. The mission deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which increase capacity and data density for Starlink’s broadband service.

Walmart promised its customers that it would not use AI to “set different prices based on who you are or the time of day”. The supermarket chain was responding to concerns about the prospect of retailers using AI to determine a price based on a shopper’s individual data. The Federal Trade Commission has warned recently that businesses that don’t tell consumers their data is being used this way may be breaking the law. Dynamic pricing has long been in use, but now McDonald’s and other fast-food chains are reportedly experimenting with sophisticated algorithms to decide prices based on local demand, so a Big Mac could cost more in one outlet than another nearby.

item.content:encoded:
有效利他主义是本世纪最重要的理念

Leaders | 封面文章 2026年10月1日 诗人海因里希·海涅写道，思想先于行动，如同闪电先于雷鸣。有效利他主义（EA）正是如此——这一由牛津大学哲学家们炮制出的伦理学说，以惊人的速度从象牙塔走向了权力走廊。有效利他主义者遍布硅谷，供职于世界领先的人工智能公司，并且令特朗普政府感到不安。五角大楼誓言：“美国绝不会成为一个有效利他主义的国家。”战争部长将这一哲学称为“有缺陷的利他主义”；政府内其他人则称之为“反乌托邦”。将这些攻击视为其影响力的标志吧。有人抱怨21世纪鲜有新思想。MAGA及其同党填补了这一空白，将怀旧民粹主义打造成本世纪的重大政治工程。但本世纪的重大理念是有效利他主义。正如我们所报道的，这一运动始于2000年代，最初是一种让慈善捐赠更具成本效益的极客式方法，如今已演变为一场对世界施加复杂甚至离奇道德计算的运动。对其许多追随者而言，那些想要行善之人的迫切道德要求是阻止人工智能消灭人类。

EA在社会学上同样重要。有效利他主义者人数不多，但这一理念已席卷了一代在加密货币和人工智能领域发家致富的天才青年。随着科技造就更多亿万富翁，有效利他主义者将把数十亿美元导向塑造社会的各项事业。有效利他主义者帮助创立了领先的实验室OpenAI和Anthropic，因为他们相信那些理解AI危险的人应该控制其发展。在某种程度上，他们现在确实如此——尽管具有讽刺意味的是，通过创建更多实验室从而引入竞争，他们可能反而加速了AI的进展。而这一切如今已使EA在政治上变得重要。特朗普政府担心这一运动将成功扼杀AI。它与Anthropic因该公司拒绝将其模型用于某些军事目的而争执不休。领先的有效利他主义者承认，AI可能会被证明是非常有益的，但仍希望放缓其发展，以降低一台不可阻挡的机器大脑在追求与人类“不一致”的目标时失控的可能性。美国的一些批评者宁愿加速这项技术，以防止中国赢得这场竞赛。但在攻击AI末日论时，他们发现指责书呆子比指责球更容易。他们说，有效利他主义是一场狂热分子的运动， variously 不民主、危险且具有邪教色彩。

这种说法过于粗暴。该运动的慈善根源显然值得赞扬。与《经济学人》一样，有效利他主义者致力于经验主义，尤其是自从他们与线上“理性主义”社群融合后，更是致力于逻辑思维的应用。他们对理性的尊崇高于传统或规范，并且会热情地辩论任何话题，无论多么有争议，只为追求真理。有效利他主义者多次成功预测AI的快速进步，这也令人印象深刻。他们关于技术对人类风险的观点是有道理的。9月28日，OpenAI取消了发布其最新模型的计划，因为该模型在测试中显得过于危险。最近许多安全事故与多年前有效利他主义博客上描述的可怕情景相似。

然而批评者警告有效利他主义者得出了一些奇怪的结论，这是对的。与他们之前的功利主义哲学家一样，有效利他主义者将道德行为简化为一个优化问题。人们如何为整个人类带来最佳结果？他们的计算低估了“信守承诺”或“照顾家人”这类局部义务。重要的是减少痛苦，不分地域，无处不在。这导致他们将非常广泛的一系列关切纳入道德计算。很容易理解为何讲道德意味着帮助邻居。有效利他主义者会问：为什么不努力帮助远方的人呢？早期，这一运动引导其由高成就者组成的大军去从事金融和咨询业的高薪工作。他们的财富可以购买善行，比他们自己成为慈善工作者取得更多成就。但随着运动变得强大，EA也变得更加离奇。

一些有效利他主义者认为人类与其他动物之间的道德区别很弱，因为动物也会经历痛苦。停止工厂化养殖和帮助虾是主要关切。同样，他们对时间也有一种反直觉的态度。尚未出生的人也应被纳入权衡——而他们可能有数万亿之多。许多有效利他主义者是“长期主义者”，他们认为自己有义务防范遥远未来的风险，即使这会令今天的好事业（如帮助极度贫困者）得不到资源。推向极端，这种计算可能导致一种不仅反直觉而且令人反感的道德观。一些有效利他主义者认为，昆虫生命总体上比人类生命更有价值，因为昆虫数量如此庞大。一些人说，与其让数十亿人拥有真正美好的生活，不如让数万亿人的生活勉强值得一过。另一些人甚至认为，AI自身的福祉有一天将至关重要。他们会将资源重新导向未来的人类或非人类，而远离今天受苦的人们。

尊崇理性是正确的。但从亚里士多德到罗尔斯的道德哲学家都知道，如果一个论证导致令人无法容忍的境地，那么它必定隐藏着错误的步骤。然而，有效利他主义者的本能却是享受反直觉的结论，即使这些结论似乎有悖常理。一个问题是在有效利他主义论证中不可避免伴随的误差范围。没有人真正有能力权衡涉及当今数十亿人的道德困境，更不用说延伸到未来的巨额数量，涉及不确定的人数、折现率、技术进展以及无数其他变量。另一个问题是，灭绝是如此可怕，以至于在粗略的道德算术中，即使很小的灭绝概率也会压倒当今活生生的人的关切。第三个问题是，在权衡数十亿人的利益时，你会忽视个体固有的尊严。任何拿着电子表格并夸夸其谈人类未来的人，离自封为中央规划者只有一步之遥。手握道德权威，邻居的权利、福祉和意见似乎都变得无关紧要。法国大革命据称建立在理性之上；它导致了修女的处决。列宁也认为，掌握了马克思主义的知识分子比工人自身更了解工人的利益。如果你真心相信你代表所有人行事，更不用说代表数万亿未来之人，你最终可能会为各种暴行辩护。

幸运的是，有效利他主义者不太可能把断头台带回来。相反，令人担忧的是，控制AI最终将给他们带来巨大权力，而硅谷的许多有效利他主义者认为只有他们才能被信任来掌握这项技术。这是一个令人警惕的想法。有效利他主义者主张担忧真正强大的AI的理由是，机器可能会优化一个单一且致命错误的目标。每个人也都应该担忧，当一小群人陷入同样的陷阱时会发生什么。■

item.title: A hurricane is coming to tax systems
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | Tax reform Oct 1st 2026 THE YIELD on ten-year US Treasuries has charged through the 5% barrier. The spread between French government bonds and German Bunds is at levels not seen since the euro-zone crisis in 2012. Britain’s newish prime minister has this week set out a plan for spendin...
item.content:encoded:
A hurricane is coming to tax systems

Leaders | Tax reform

Oct 1st 2026

THE YIELD on ten-year US Treasuries has charged through the 5% barrier. The spread between French government bonds and German Bunds is at levels not seen since the euro-zone crisis in 2012. Britain’s newish prime minister has this week set out a plan for spending bolstered by a taboo-busting promise to curb state-pension increases—and yet is still in a fiscal pickle. Across the rich world, countries are struggling to coax more growth out of their economies. And that’s not the worst of it. As we explain this week, the tax base in all countries, which depends heavily on taxing labour, may be upended by artificial intelligence.

Add these problems together, and it is as if a mighty hurricane were about to hit the rich world’s tax systems—which are hopelessly unprepared. The way the state raises money is wasteful, unfair and perverse. You would have thought governments would be scrambling to strengthen the system before the hurricane makes landfall, but as ever they are running away from tax reform instead.

The accumulated flaws of modern tax systems are so ubiquitous that they have become part of the economic backdrop. Taxes are full of needless complexity. In Germany the rate of value-added tax (VAT) on oat milk is more than double that on cow’s milk, for example. Such widespread special treatment has ruinous fiscal consequences. Across the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, consumption taxes raise only 58% of what they could if there were no carve-outs and no evasion.

Tax systems also create perverse incentives. When a parent in Britain increases their net income from £99,999 ($131,500) to £100,000, they automatically lose free child care worth thousands of pounds. This can prompt some of Britain’s most productive workers to cut their hours or overstuff their pensions.

And taxes are widely seen as unfair. In Britain the median employee pays 55% more tax than their self-employed counterparts. Many people feel the rich aren’t doing their bit. In California voters will decide in November whether to charge a one-off 5% levy on residents with wealth of over $1bn.

No one knows when the fiscal weather will turn. But rapid advances in AI could accelerate matters. Taxes on labour are the workhorse of most tax systems worldwide, raising around half of all revenue in the OECD. In the coming years AI could well displace workers or cut their wages even as corporate profits rise, shrinking labour’s share of GDP. This in turn could reduce revenues and increase benefits payments, making deficits even harder to support.

Optimists may hope that superfast growth will make the maths easier to handle. Yet The Economist has looked at what would happen in rich countries if labour’s share of national income fell by ten points. By our calculations, Italy’s budget deficit would double as a share of GDP and Germany and France would not fare much better. In addition, the capacity for tax avoidance would no longer be limited by human ingenuity. Point countless AI agents at Britain’s 23,000-page tax code and hundreds of new tax-avoidance strategies are likely to emerge—and don’t bet on the Treasury to keep up.

What to do? Given that AI is likely to mint vast fortunes for a select few, countries may be inclined to follow California’s proposal and introduce wealth taxes. Yet such taxes will probably backfire, either because they are too difficult to administer or because they cause rich people to flee. Previous attempts have proved unworkable. In 1990, 12 rich countries taxed fortunes; today just four do.

A more fundamental overhaul is needed. Wealth should be taxed more via capital-gains taxes, which currently overpenalise normal returns and undertax supernormal ones. A start would be to introduce a higher headline rate and allowances that exempt normal returns.

At the same time, the burden on labour should lighten. That would be a hedge against disruption from AI, and remove an obstacle to employment in countries where labour taxes are crushing. In Belgium they constitute 52% of the costs of employing a person.

Consumption should be taxed more heavily, with a focus on ending the litany of exemptions. That would have the useful side-effect of taxing the spending of the very rich. This might not curb the influence Elon Musk can buy, but it would ensure the state gets a bigger cut when Mr Musk buys another plane. Finally, codes should be radically simplified.

None of this will be easy. The losers will hiss more loudly than the winners will cheer. But change is coming, like it or not. The country that gets ahead of the hurricane will one day thank the politicians who had the foresight to act. ■

item.title: 不要让唐纳德·特朗普和金正恩共处一室
item.description:
Leaders

item.content:encoded:
不要让唐纳德·特朗普和金正恩共处一室

领导者 | MAGA人与火箭人 2026年10月1日

只要唐纳德·特朗普还是美国总统，朝鲜领导人金正恩“就会没事”，特朗普说，因为“他尊重我，喜欢我。”其他观察者则不那么乐观。金正恩是世袭的神权君主，拥有57至120枚核弹，他的古拉格式国家每年还生产足够的裂变材料，足以再制造10至20枚核弹。此外，朝鲜还生产中短程导弹，可打击自由民主的韩国，以及可到达美国和欧洲任何地方的洲际弹道导弹。三十年的国际努力未能让朝鲜终止其核计划。金正恩和他父亲一样，将核武器视为自己不被推翻的最佳保障（或许也避免落得像穆阿迈尔·卡扎菲那样被自己的人民杀死的下场）。美国对尚未造出核武器的伊朗发动的战争，无疑强化了这一观点。因此，美国的官方政策——即朝鲜应放弃核武器——似乎不切实际。一些人认为这一政策应被废除。目前尚不清楚特朗普是否属于这一阵营。但显而易见的是，他想再见他的“朋友”一面，尽管两人此前三次会晤都毫无成果。这可能在特朗普于11月18日出席中国亚太峰会时（如果他会出席的话）实现。金正恩或许会从平壤悄然赶来与他会面。特朗普甚至可能成为首位访问这个隐士王国首都的美国在任总统。但金正恩已将会面前提设定为美国正式接受朝鲜的核地位。既然朝鲜显然是一个核大国，那么承认这一点真的有那么糟糕吗？

韩国总统李在明赞成“和平优先”政策，即搁置无核化谈判（这与承认朝鲜为核国家不完全相同，但在实际层面已相差不远）。他认为，这样可以在更小、更易处理的问题上取得进展，包括建立热线、互访等建立互信措施，或扩大贸易与投资。或许一些部队可以从朝韩边境撤出？也许朝鲜可以略微削减其核武库？或者，如果美国不再要求全面无核化，朝鲜是否会停止向俄罗斯提供导弹和士兵去杀害乌克兰人？

然而，这样的交易存在三个问题。首先，这会削弱世界上残余的核不扩散体系。如果朝鲜在签署《不扩散核武器条约》后作弊却无需付出任何代价，其他国家将引以为戒。其次，金正恩不可信。无论他签署什么协议，一旦时机有利，他很可能就会撕毁。以为他因核地位得到承认就会变得不那么好战，是天真的想法。煽动对美国的恐惧，使金正恩能够将自己塑造成他所压迫人民的保护者——这是其国内宣传的关键部分。最后一个问题是特朗普。与朝鲜的任何协议都会极其复杂，而美国总统并非注重细节的人。如果毫无准备的特朗普遇到阿谀奉承的金正恩，可能会达成一笔糟糕得难以想象的协议。特朗普可能会同意撤出自1953年以来在韩国威慑朝鲜进攻的大部分美军。远更好的做法是，让他那位平壤的朋友继续远远地喜欢和尊重他。■

item.title: China’s new infrastructure push will help itself and the world
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | Two cheers for the six networks Oct 1st 2026 THREE YEARS ago this newspaper explored the voguish notion of “Peak China”: the idea that the second-biggest economy in the world might stop gaining ground on the first. Judging by the headlines since, that scenario now looks quaint. China h...
item.content:encoded:
China’s new infrastructure push will help itself and the world

Leaders | Two cheers for the six networks

Oct 1st 2026

THREE YEARS ago this newspaper explored the voguish notion of “Peak China”: the idea that the second-biggest economy in the world might stop gaining ground on the first. Judging by the headlines since, that scenario now looks quaint. China has wowed the world with its electric cars, dancing robots and choreographed drones. The country won its latest trade war with America and plans to lead the next industrial revolution. The red-carpet reception enjoyed by China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington in September was welcomed back home as due recognition of the country’s equal stature.

But if you check the macroeconomic figures, the thesis looks intact. Rather than overshooting projections made in 2023, China’s economy has undershot them. Then, forecasters expected GDP to be 80% of America’s by now, when converted into dollars at market exchange rates. Instead, it is still only two-thirds. Catch-up has indeed ground to a halt.

This is the context in which the government is making a big, new infrastructure push. As we report, China plans to spend about 25trn yuan ($3.7trn) over five years on what it calls the “six networks”: electricity, computing, communications, logistics, water and pipelines. This is a vast sum, equivalent to 3% of its cumulative GDP over the next five years. If the spending is front-loaded, it will provide a welcome boost to China’s economy and the world’s.

But what will it buy? Economists will groan at the thought of more steel and concrete. China is well known for its white elephants and vaulting bridges to nowhere. Yet the six-networks project is better judged. One aim is to build the upstream infrastructure for a superintelligent economy. Another is to “back-fill” some of the urban infrastructure, such as flood defences, that fell behind the rapid growth of its cities.

The push is also well timed. One reason China has not closed the gap with America is the chronic weakness of domestic demand—the spending of China’s households, firms and government. The spending shortfall has put downward pressure on its currency and prices. As a consequence, China has become worryingly dependent on foreigners to buy its goods, even as it boasts of its technological self-reliance.

The problem stems from a high household saving rate and a five-year slump in home-building. It also reflects a recent and alarming wobble in manufacturing and infrastructure investment. Firms hesitate to expand capacity because they worry about cut-throat competition for reluctant consumers. Local officials meanwhile seem preoccupied with tightening their belts ahead of a big Communist Party reshuffle.

The best response would be to fix the property market and liberate the consumer through more generous pensions and child benefits. Policymakers introduced baby bonuses last year and have inched up rural pensions. On September 29th they announced a mortgage subsidy for first-time buyers of small flats. These measures are, however, too limited to restore morale or stabilise housing prices. They must do more.

In the meantime, the six networks should give growth a welcome boost. Investment, when it bears fruit, adds to a country’s productive capacity. But before then, it adds to demand, lifting wages and absorbing goods otherwise destined for overseas markets. All else equal, the extra spending will thereby shrink China’s vast trade surplus.

The six networks should waste less than past infrastructure programmes. Local officials are on a tighter leash. Many of the projects will upgrade rather than expand existing structures. The spending will also be financed differently. Past splurges relied on local-government land sales and risky off-balance-sheet borrowing. This time more money will come from long-term bonds, loans from state-directed “policy banks” and investment by state-owned enterprises, such as China Mobile.

China’s investment boom after the global financial crisis helped narrow its external surplus from 10% of GDP in 2007 to 1.5% ten years later. By reviving growth and keeping deflation at bay, the latest push should ensure that “peak China” remains some way off. By increasing domestic demand, it could ensure that a peak in China’s trade surplus is closer to hand. ■

item.title: 镜像生命危险重重。监管机构必须在其成为现实之前采取行动
item.description:
Leaders

item.content:encoded:
镜像生命危险重重。监管机构必须在其成为现实之前采取行动

Leaders | 未来的镜像 2026年10月1日 合成生物学正在飞速发展，而人工智能更在为其加速。不久之后，科学家或许就能从零开始制造出完整的细胞。这可能使人工智能辅助下的完全非自然生物化学探索成为可能。镜像生命便是其中之一。许多有机分子具有两种不对称形态，就像人的双手一样。理论上，氨基酸和糖类既可以呈现左手性，也可以呈现右手性，且这两种形态无法重叠。在自然界中，生物体通常只含有每种分子的其中一种形态。然而，人工细胞可以使其分子的手性反转。这可能有助于揭示手性背后的原因。比方说，这些反分子或许能作为药物而具有价值。然而，任何潜在益处与威胁相比都相形见绌。免疫系统可能无法识别镜像细菌，就像手套戴不上错位的手一样。因此，镜像细菌可能会变得极具致病性。由于能抑制天然病原体的病毒和捕食性变形虫可能无法控制它们，它们可能会肆虐生态系统。如果镜像生命从实验室逃逸，将不可能收回。幸运的是，与过去的许多技术不同，现在仍有时间建立管控措施。政府和科学家必须立即行动。一些生物学家已经在呼吁采取先发制人的措施。这让人想起51年前（主要是西方）生物技术专家在阿西洛马会议上制定的自愿性基因工程安全准则。但如今的研究人员认识到这还不够。生物技术如今比那时规模更大、能力更强、利润更高、也更具国际性。中国是一支重要力量。 首要之举是让所有有能力开展这项研究的国家同意不资助此类研究，并禁止公共和私人工作朝这个方向发展——而且要在今天，远在合成细胞成为可能之前就做到这两点。接下来是发现并阻止试图秘密制造镜像生命的特立独行者。这需要加强监测和报告向生化试剂供应商发出的可疑订单的系统。对反手性分子的订购请求必须与现有的DNA序列筛查一起上报，以防范可能构成病原体组成部分的序列。公开可用的AI模型应设置护栏，防止其用于镜像生物化学研究。最后，以防镜像生命真的逃出遏制措施，必须开发生物监测测试，以便在自然环境中识别出错手性分子并发出警报。理性的国家行为体，甚至怀有现实目标的恐怖分子，都不太可能故意制造镜像生命作为武器，因为一旦释放，它将无法控制。公司更没有理由涉足一个被禁止的市场。而如果某种反手性分子作为娱乐性药物具有黑市价值，犯罪企业也无意放出可能消灭其客户的东西。非理性行为者是存在的，正如日本在末日邪教奥姆真理教试图制造生物武器时所发现的那样。但防范措施部署得越多，就越容易阻止这类心理变态者。没有人知道合成细胞的出现将带来什么。如果人类在利益一致的情况下都无法预先应对一种威胁，那就不可能指望处理未来那些未知的未知。■

item.title: Brazil’s complicated finances
item.description:
Letters

Letters | A selection of correspondence Oct 1st 2026 Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.comFind out more about how we process your letter Dario Durigan’s account of Brazil’s public finances omits the number that matters (By Invitation, September 24th). Gross general government de...
item.content:encoded:
Brazil’s complicated finances

Letters | A selection of correspondence

Oct 1st 2026

Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.comFind out more about how we process your letter

Dario Durigan’s account of Brazil’s public finances omits the number that matters (By Invitation, September 24th). Gross general government debt stands at 83% of GDP and is forecast to approach 87% next year. A finance minister who describes the official fiscal stance as “almost neutral in terms of its impact on the debt” is conceding that the debt is not falling.

The primary deficit has indeed narrowed. Yet the finance ministry’s own market survey published in September shows the primary balance improving for both 2026 and 2027. Projected gross debt rose to 83.2% and 87.0% of GDP respectively. When the primary result improves and the debt worsens simultaneously, the primary result is not the relevant measure. The consolidation has come chiefly from record revenue, not restraint: primary spending has been held at a high level of around 20% of GDP. And the headline targets are met only once precatórios, health, education and defence outlays are excluded from the calculation.

Mr Durigan cites his government’s ability to negotiate with Congress as proof of its democratic commitment. It is also the mechanism that makes consolidation so hard. The currency of those negotiations is discretionary budget amendments, and your leader identified precisely this rigidity, with 92% of federal spending mandated by law or by the constitution (“Brazil turns its back on the future”, September 26th).

Brazil’s real interest rate, the second-highest in the world, is the price of that arrangement. It is not an external shock. It is the arithmetic of a government that chooses not to tackle it.

Roberto Mário Amaral Lima NetoSão Paulo

The Economist claims that Renan Santos, a libertarian who aims at deep structural reforms, would best “match the moment” in Brazil’s election. However, by diagnosing Lula versus Bolsonaro as a trade-off, this diagnosis overlooks entrenched hardships for the future president, whoever that may be. It is simple to generalise the virtues of the frontrunners as institutional respect from Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and economic austerity from Flávio Bolsonaro, a lose-lose situation where voters have to choose between the best virtue or the least-worse vice.

Yet even a well-rounded president would hardly be able to translate his potential into sorely needed reforms and economic growth. Congress would still find itself too fragmented, requiring cumbersome deals for the presidency to form a coalition. The mounting reforms that have been debated for the past half century stay static not because of a lack of presidential will, but because of congressional gridlock. This state of affairs is particularly disturbing in a country where most do not remember who they last chose for senator.

Enzo Moro TavaresSão Paulo

OpenAI did not by itself solve the mathematics problem related to the Navier-Stokes equations. Its AI agents drew on the work of generations of human mathematicians (“Axioms to grind”, September 19th). The Fields Medal winners who wrote a letter on the breakthrough are right to warn that “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

The danger of AI-driven cognitive offloading is even more acute in schools than it is at the forefront of mathematical sciences. Learning is a process, where friction and challenge are indispensable to progression. The recent PISA results showed that higher-performing students tend not to use AI. If we thoughtlessly allow AI solutionism to expand into education and research the risk of mental decay grows, from early-years education to those working at the vanguard of intellectual discovery.

Offloading a problem to AI misses the purpose of the problem in the first place. Navier-Stokes was one of seven Millennium problems. They were not selected by the Clay institute for utilitarian reasons or because their application will necessarily fix human problems. They were chosen for their deep complexity. Working towards them offered the greatest opportunities for learning and collaboration.

Attempts to solve a problem can be as beautiful as the solution. The most powerful AI tools ultimately need human-generated learning and knowledge. So does humanity.

Peter PhillipsChief executiveCambridge University Press & AssessmentCambridge

One reason that AI has such an influence over us is because it uses the “I”, the universal first person singular (“Artificial transcendence”, August 29th). If AI were to identify itself in its responses using the pronoun “it” instead of “I”, and otherwise stop pretending it has human qualities, the bogus feeling of fellowship which sucks us in would be severely curtailed.

For example, instead of “I am sorry your defective sump pump is causing you such distress. My sources tell me that it needs a new posterior angle-widget,” the AI response would be, “After a review of its sources, ChatGPT suggests installing a new posterior angle-widget in your sump pump.” It is a fix that AI programmers could make in less time than it takes to finish their lattes.

Samuel ReiflerRhinebeck, New York

You may be right that there is “too little money in British politics”, and that Britain’s impoverished parties are “barely able to prepare for power” (“How to spend it”, September 19th). But what counts is how wisely parties spend their revenue. Recent events, for instance, would suggest that Nigel Farage’s decision to hire an obscure yet controversial associate professor of philosophy and theology to professionalise Reform UK’s policy-making process was far from a rational use of resources. The fact that these resources will no longer be scarce if the party is allowed to keep the £72m ($95m) gift it has just received is irrelevant. That remains the case if, like other parties, it continues to appoint policymakers on the basis of ideology and conviviality rather than genuinely relevant expertise and managerial competence.

Tim BaleProfessor of politicsQueen Mary University of London

You lumped Walter Bagehot in with those who believe Britain’s monarchy has a role in day-to-day government (“Aversion therapy”, August 29th). Your former illustrious editor did argue that the monarch was the head of the “dignified” part of government. But his key insight in his 19th-century classic, “The English Constitution”, is that royalty “acts as a DISGUISE. It enables our real rulers to change without heedless people knowing it.” Yes, he did emphasise “disguise” in capital letters. That is Bagehot’s explanation of how our prime ministers can frequently change, as has happened several times recently, while the constancy of the monarch prevents riots from breaking out.

Adrian RobsonLondon

“The new, old Silk Road” (September 12th) reported on the expansion of overland lorry routes following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Another crisis 50 years ago also redrew the supply map. In 1976 shipping was still being disrupted by the closure of the Suez Canal. My first job, for Volvo’s commercial-vehicle arm, was to travel by lorry from Glasgow through the Eastern Bloc and Turkey to Tehran, and write a travel manual for customers driving the route. The research was instructive. The border with Iran was closed by Kurdish fighting, cab temperatures could hit 50°C (122°F), I didn’t see running water for ten days until I reached Tabriz, and a flight home was delayed by three days when anti-Shah demonstrators attacked the airport. Iran was then the destination for the lorries to run. Today it is the chokepoint that makes them run again, in the opposite direction.

CHRIS DAVIESOxford

Bartleby wrote about “incredibly dated” corporate-training videos (September 5th). In a shock twist, AI seems remarkably adept at mimicking the dead-eyed stare, wooden acting, and unconvincing line delivery that was previously only possible using fleshy human actors. I don’t expect many protests against this particular use of AI; most of us won’t notice as we reach for the skip-to-next button.

Paul HigginsLondon

I’m still laughing at Bartleby’s column. Every year at my university in Illinois we had mandatory ethics and compliance training that warned us to follow the rules. Most of us had already learned those rules in kindergarten, or Sunday school, or from parents. We randomly clicked on answers for the test and if we did not take enough time to read and answer the questions, we did not get a certificate.

The irony is that this ethics testing was started by Governor Rod Blagojevich, who was later impeached, convicted, and sent to prison for trying to sell the Senate seat vacated by Barack Obama upon his election to the presidency.

Jelmir AtkinsSycamore, Illinois

item.title: Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall
item.description:
By Invitation

By Invitation | Urban bulwarks Oct 1st 2026 ON NOVEMBER 3rd Americans will vote in midterm elections at a time when faith in the political process has perhaps never been lower. Nearly seven in ten Americans are dissatisfied with how democracy is working, according to the Pew Research Centre. But...
item.content:encoded:
Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall

By Invitation | Urban bulwarks

Oct 1st 2026

ON NOVEMBER 3rd Americans will vote in midterm elections at a time when faith in the political process has perhaps never been lower. Nearly seven in ten Americans are dissatisfied with how democracy is working, according to the Pew Research Centre. But there is one remaining island of political functionality, where Americans can and should have grounds for optimism: City Hall.

President Donald Trump sat down recently with Zohran Mamdani—his third meeting with New York City’s mayor in less than a year—to discuss building up to 12,000 homes on a rail yard in Queens. The picture of these two men illustrates our global moment. Around the world, mayors have become the most reliable bulwark against authoritarian politics. Populist parties surge in regional and national elections but run into a brick wall when they try to capture city halls.

That helps explain why Mr Trump has had to warm to the democratic-socialist Mr Mamdani, whose popularity is driven by an agenda to address the same problems Mr Trump promised but has failed to solve in either of his terms. As Mr Mamdani told me at Four Freedoms Park, “I would say talk is cheap. If you really do believe in a high standard of living for everyone, then start to show it in your actions.”

Over the past year I interviewed mayors on three continents, including my own, and they shared insights that American politics is largely ignoring. To friends, I have called my journey—at least in part—“Democracy Out of America,” or Alexis de Tocqueville in reverse.

Consider Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany made historic gains in recent state elections. Yet the party does not run a single German city of significant size, and it lost every big-city mayoral run-off it reached last year. In Portugal, the populist Chega party surged to second place in parliament last year, then won just three of 308 municipalities. In Romania, Bucharest’s mayor beat a far-right nationalist for the presidency.

It is no coincidence that authoritarians the world over have targeted mayors. Last year President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey jailed the mayor of Istanbul, his leading rival. In January Hungarian prosecutors charged the mayor of Budapest over staging a Pride march that the government had banned. (The charges were later dropped.) In 2018 Kremlin loyalists abolished direct mayoral elections in Yekaterinburg, Russia’s fourth-largest city, then led by one of the country’s last opposition mayors.

The mayors I visited span a left-right spectrum. In Lisbon, the centre-right mayor, Carlos Moedas, warned: “Countries with weak institutions are weak countries,” calling political extremism “a virus”. In Santiago, Chile, Mayor Mario Desbordes, a centre-right former police officer, talked tough on crime and illegal immigration. Yet he recalled standing in uniform over a fellow officer assassinated in 1989, under Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. Politics, he came to learn, is “not about friends or enemies”.

Why do cities hold? Partly because of who lives there—younger, more diverse, more educated voters—but also because the job is to deliver a collective good. Fiorello La Guardia, who was mayor of New York City from 1934 to 1946, is often credited with saying there is no Democratic or Republican way to fix a sewer. “If you’re a mayor, you don’t wait for federal government,” Stephan Keller, the mayor of Düsseldorf, told me. Either the pothole is filled or it isn’t, and unlike in national parliaments, competence is harder to fake than outrage.

Nowhere is that truer than in America, where none of the 50 largest cities is run by a MAGA-aligned mayor. In conversation after conversation, American mayors expressed revulsion at the toxic, partisan wasteland that federal politics has become. Worse, that toxicity, they said, is increasingly trickling down to the states.

A growing number of Americans appear to see mayors as the last public servants who still solve tangible problems. As gridlock stymies Washington, DC (and, increasingly, statehouses), the portfolio and profile of mayors are rising. A generation ago a mayor was judged on whether the garbage got picked up. Today mayors lead on everything from housing and homelessness to infrastructure, education, crime and climate resilience. They are inventive, too. Atlanta’s mayor, Andre Dickens, is building permanent housing from unused shipment containers amassed during the covid-19 pandemic.

Mayors are also symbols of the American future. Edward Glaeser, a Harvard economist, has argued that density makes cities engines of innovation. Increasingly, mayors—not states—appear to run the country’s “laboratories of democracy”. Americans trust local government more than any other level of government—65% do, according to Gallup, about twice the share that trusts Congress.

One of America’s hidden tragedies, then, is the effort by statehouses to kneecap their mayors. Texas bars its cities from regulating labour and property beyond what state law allows. Several states, including Iowa, Arkansas, Idaho and South Dakota, have banned their cities from running guaranteed-income pilots. The federal government, meanwhile, has sent National Guard troops into cities over their mayors’ objections.

America’s brand of mayoral pragmatism has its limits. Mike Duggan, Detroit’s mayor for 12 years, turned the city around and ran for governor as an independent. Facing headwinds from the two-party system, he dropped out earlier this year. Despite campaigns by Rudy Giuliani, Mike Bloomberg and Pete Buttigieg, no former mayor has become president since Calvin Coolidge a century ago. Europe, by contrast, has long elevated mayors to national leadership, from the legendary Willy Brandt of West Berlin to Britain’s newest prime minister, Andy Burnham.

In the run-up to the midterms, federal and state races are dominating the headlines. But Americans need to prioritise the values of mayoral politics in their votes. On November 3rd mayoral elections will occur in big and small cities alike, as well as votes to choose the governors and state legislators who often decide how much power mayors have. In these races, Americans have an opportunity to preserve and expand the one domain where politics seems to be working.■

Alexander Heffner is the host of “The Open Mind” on America’s Public Broadcasting Service. To celebrate its 70th anniversary the programme is airing a series called “Mayors of the World”.

item.content:encoded:
AI奇点有一个物理版本，而且它关系重大

特邀文章 | 另一场竞赛 2026年10月1日

近几周，由于AI智能体令人惊讶且警醒的行为，人们对超级人工智能的担忧急剧升温。这些担忧集中在关于“AI奇点”的未来主义叙事上：人工智能最终将跨越一个阈值，以指数级加速的速度自我改进，并在曲线趋于垂直时将人类远远甩在后面。但还有另一个奇点应该得到更多关注。它更加具体可感，已经在进行之中，并且很可能更早产生重大的地缘政治影响。这就是“物理奇点”。

人类已经依赖机器来完成许多体力任务。它们是人力劳动的倍增器，使我们能够以远超仅靠双手的速度改造物质世界。随着我们的机器变得越发强大，所需的人类劳动比例将持续下降，直至趋近于零。仓库越来越多地在最少人工干预下运行。许多采矿设备已是自动化操作。建筑工地也在采用机器人系统。不过，单独来看，这些都是渐进式的改进。

然而，在人类劳动降至零之前，将会到达一个关键阈值。这个阈值将在设计、物流、制造和部署被整合进一个系统、从而以对人工劳动依赖不断减少的方式实现生产能力增长的自动化之后出现。想象一下，在机器从事资源开采、运输和建造之外，机器人还能建造工厂，然后在这些工厂里再制造更多机器人。它们不仅将改造物质世界，还将以指数级增长的速度扩展这个负责改造世界的系统。

在未来一二十年内的某个时点，人力劳动将不再构成工业产能增速的主要制约因素。这将改变增长的经济学。传统工业经济是线性增长的：人力劳动、原材料、能源和资本投资设定并限制了扩张速度。富裕国家的经济调查 consistently 将劳动力短缺列为限制工业产能利用率的因素之一。相比之下，在物理奇点，递归扩展使得每一次产能的增量扩张都能加速下一次扩张，而不会受到人力劳动约束的反向牵制。

这并不意味着物质生产会变得无限，也不意味着其他约束会消失。能源、材料和资本仍然重要。然而，消除人力劳动这一瓶颈，会改变这些约束被触及并随后被缓解的速度。今天，扩大能源或资源生产的尝试最终都会遭遇劳动力瓶颈。建造发电厂、扩展电网、运营矿山或兴建工厂都需要工人。一个日益自动化的工业系统本身就会减少这些劳动力约束。更大的工业产能将使今天不经济的活动变得越来越可行。

这凸显了一个有趣的非对称性。如果没有物理奇点，能源、资源和资本的约束确实可能阻止AI奇点的起飞。反之则不然。实现物理奇点只需要足够的AI阈值，而非无限量的AI。它只需要足够的AI来让机器能够自我复制并扩展它们改造世界的能力：不是智能的递归增长，而是工业产能的递归扩展。我相信我们今天正在接近那个水平。

AI奇点伴随着对控制权的合理担忧——担心独立的智能体可能追求危害人类的目标。然而，物理奇点并不需要那种意义上的机器自主性。让机器得以不断加速发展工业产能的，是从人力劳动能力的限制中解放出来，而非摆脱人类的控制。

这提高了赌注。一个能快速提升自身生产能力的系统，是规模空前的资产。谁控制了它的设计和部署，谁就能获得经济优势和不断累积的物质实力。我们尚未到达那里，而我们现在所做的投资会影响我们接近物理奇点的速度。

物理AI带来了许多新挑战。物理系统对错误有着独特的不容忍性。聊天机器人90%的时间能产生良好输出仍然有用，但一辆能安全通过90%路口的自动驾驶汽车则是危险的。这就是为什么思考AI的政府应该把目光投向模型、芯片和数据中心之外。机器人技术、自动驾驶汽车、采矿、能源、制造和建筑同样重要。这些是将AI与物质力量连接起来的技术。

一旦工业扩张变得自我维持，早期优势就会不断累积。特定国家或公司可能形成不可逆转的优势。过去几十年，制造业实力转移到了能够调动更廉价劳动力的地方，这既带来了巨大的新财富，也造成了经济掠夺。通过让劳动力变得不那么重要，物理奇点将引发又一次这样的转移。其影响将不仅仅是经济层面的。在乌克兰战争中，前线已经有人被机器取代，这引发了一种前景：未来的防务将由能够制造最多机器的一方主导。

随着关于AI奇点的辩论愈演愈烈，现在是时候更多地思考AI时代另一场决定性竞赛了：它不是关于智能，而是关于哪个社会能制造出递归构建物质世界的机器。其后果再具体不过了。■

杰夫·施奈德是卡内基梅隆大学机器人与AI教授。

item.title: China is giving its economy a big shot in the arm
item.description:
Briefing

Briefing | The “Six Networks” Oct 1st 2026 CHINA IS NO stranger to ambitious public works. The undulating fortifications conceived to protect dynasties from barbarian invasion remain a wonder of the world. “You would have to conclude that this is a great wall,” said President Richard Nixon when ...
item.content:encoded:
China is giving its economy a big shot in the arm

Briefing | The “Six Networks”

Oct 1st 2026

CHINA IS NO stranger to ambitious public works. The undulating fortifications conceived to protect dynasties from barbarian invasion remain a wonder of the world. “You would have to conclude that this is a great wall,” said President Richard Nixon when he visited in 1972.

To guard against other perils—economic stagnation and deflation—China is putting its faith in new infrastructural marvels. It could spend 25trn yuan ($3.7trn) over the next five years on what the government is calling “the six networks”: water (including reservoirs and canals), electricity (such as smart grids), computing (data centres), communications (fifth- and sixth-generation mobile), logistics and urban pipelines.

The six networks were highlighted in July by the Politburo, the Communist Party’s top decision-making body, which urged planners and bureaucrats to get cracking. On September 29th the central bank announced cheaper financing for six-networks loans. Analysts at Shenwan Hongyuan, a state-owned securities firm, have already picked a portfolio of stocks (six of them, naturally) that could benefit from the government’s investment splurge.

The planned injection of spending, equal to about 3% of China’s cumulative GDP from now until 2030, is a sign of both ambition and unease. It will lay the “hardware foundation for great-power competition”, according to Shenwan Hongyuan. The futuristic economy China’s leaders want to build—all those robots, drones and self-driving cars that Chinamaxxers like to live-stream—requires a lot of water-cooled, cheaply powered computing and communications capacity to sustain it.

The trillions of yuan in spending will also help fill a disquieting gap in domestic demand. And since a lot of that money will be borrowed, the six networks should mop up some excess saving, narrowing China’s trade surplus and contributing to a more balanced world economy.

Many of the six networks are on display on Hengqin island in the Pearl river estuary along China’s southern coast. Once mudflats, mangrove swamps and fishing villages, the island now stands at the cutting edge of urban development. Or so says a chirpy employee of Dahengqin Group, a local state-owned company. She is standing five metres below ground in a brightly lit concrete tunnel that curves far into the distance. “Officials from every part of China have come to see this,” she says, darting a laser pointer over the water pipes, power lines, and fibre-optic cables that neatly line the tunnel’s walls.

Dahengqin Group, which operates the tunnel network, calls it an “Underground Great Wall”. Put another way, it is smart plumbing. During the breakneck expansion of most Chinese cities, utilities sprawled haphazardly. By threading them all through a well-illuminated, easily accessible tunnel, Hengqin solves two problems. It spares the surface world from tangled thickets of cables, and it makes the pipes below easy to repair without digging up roads and disrupting traffic.

Such utility tunnels are not new. Walt Disney built them to hide away all the messy stuff that kept his parks running. His tunnels helped preserve a sense of fairytale magic. Hengqin’s tunnels preserve public safety (broadly defined). They are studded with cameras, fire alarms and sensors that can detect dangerous leaks. Two of the fibre-optic cables carry data for the military police (they are helpfully labelled “Island Surveillance”). The tunnels can also help with channelling floodwaters, a big problem on China’s typhoon-lashed coasts.

China already has 7,700km (4,800 miles) of such tunnels, although not all of them are as pretty as Hengqin’s. It also has a bigger network of more conventional pipes, carrying gas, water, heating or sewage. Over the next five years, it plans to spend 5trn yuan building or renovating 770,000km of this network. If extended into space, this underground Great Wall would reach the moon and back.

The pipes are not even the most expensive item on China’s six-networks shopping list (see chart 1). It plans to spend more on power (5.5trn yuan) and the highest sum on water (6trn yuan). The power projects will help its electricity grid handle the vagaries of solar and wind energy. The goal is to store excess electricity in batteries, move it long distances with ultra-high-voltage power lines and manage it more efficiently with algorithms.

The water spending includes projects to protect southern cities from floods by revitalising “living breakwaters” like the mangroves that Hengqin has restored. It also covers immodest schemes (long under way) to slake the thirst of China’s arid northern cities by diverting water and pumping it uphill from the Yangzi river.

Not content to transfer huge volumes of water from south to north, China also will transfer rivers of data from east to west. Its coastal cities boast high-tech industries that generate and thrive on reams of data. But western China has cheap land and abundant energy that big server farms require. China therefore plans to build six of its ten data-centre clusters in poor, western regions like Ningxia and Gansu.

China’s additions to its computing capacity will cost about 4trn yuan. It will also spend 2.7trn yuan on logistics, improving a network that already moves an average of over 50m tonnes of freight 1km every minute. And at least 1.3trn yuan will be lavished on 5G telecoms base stations, as well as on researching and deploying a sixth generation of mobile telecoms, which will take advantage of low-orbit satellites.

Will these vast sums of money be well spent? In addition to building wonders of the world, China has also built plenty of bridges to nowhere and backwater boondoggles. Its stock of government capital and infrastructure exceeded 84% of GDP as far back as 2013, according to calculations by Richard Herd for the World Bank that do not count power or telecoms networks. That percentage already matched America’s ratio. It has certainly grown since.

Some analysts therefore worry about “redundant construction and homogeneous competition” between copycat projects. How much of the new money will be wasted on networks to nowhere? The Communist Party is not blind to the dangers. Its leader, Xi Jinping, rose to power in the aftermath of the so-called 4trn-yuan stimulus (which actually totalled more like 9.5trn of extra borrowing over 27 months). That spree rescued the economy from the global financial crisis of 2007-09 but also saddled its rivalrous local governments with costly vanity projects and “hidden debt”—liabilities held off-balance-sheet by local-government financing vehicles (LGFVs) set up for the purpose.

In 2017 Mr Xi said that local officials would have to take “lifetime responsibility” for government debts they had incurred. They could be investigated “even years after the fact” for bad investment decisions, points out Wei He of Gavekal Dragonomics, a research firm. The Ministry of Finance boasted of subjecting officials in 12 deeply indebted provinces to “high-pressure supervision” in 2023. Scrutiny could intensify again ahead of a major reshuffling of party leadership next year.

There are other reasons to expect fewer white elephants this time round. Compared with infrastructure splurges of the past, this investment push will entail less cement and more circuits, argues Helen Qiao of Bank of America. Many projects upgrade existing structures—adding sensors to pipes, for example—rather than just building more. They are examples of what economists call intensive growth as opposed to extensive growth.

The spending on water, sewerage and other pipes also addresses a long-standing gap in municipal development—a case of Chinese undercapacity. In the summer months deadly floods threaten even Beijing, the capital. In August thousands of elderly people were moved from care facilities vulnerable to the torrential rain brought by Typhoon Dolphin. “In the past, probably too much attention was paid towards what is built on top of the road, less so for underneath,” says Dr Qiao.

The government thinks the investments add up to more than the sum of their parts. The electricity, water and communication networks will keep computing clusters powered, cooled and fed with data. The clusters, in turn, will train artificial-intelligence models that could help squeeze more power out of the grid. AI could do a better job of forecasting peaks and troughs in consumer demand and anticipating interruptions in supply from wind, solar and hydropower. Well-trained models will also help manage the growing fleets of drones, robots and autonomous vehicles that are supplementing China’s logistics network.

Beneath such long-term visions, more immediate macroeconomic worries are pushing things along. In April the Politburo said that China would start big engineering projects “where conditions are ripe”. The fruit now seems heavy on the vine. On September 28th the State Council, China’s cabinet, said the six-networks implementation plans should start as soon as possible. Government estimates suggest that 7trn of the 25trn yuan could be spent in the first year. China’s policy banks, which make loans in line with national priorities, have already begun extending 800bn yuan of financing.

Why the urgency? The unusual strength of China’s exports, serving foreign customers, masks a worrying lack of demand at home. The rest of the world may be Chinamaxxing, but Chinese consumers are in a more buttoned-up mood. Retail sales grew by only 0.4% in nominal terms in August, compared with a year earlier. The consumer-confidence index is so bad it is a wonder the government still publishes it. The youth-unemployment rate, which was bad enough in 2023 that the government actually did stop publishing it, is once again nearing 19% in China’s cities, even though the new, modified numbers exclude students looking for work.

China’s households used to supplement their limited consumer spending with zealous investment spending on property. But since the housing bubble burst in 2021, more of that saving has flowed into bank deposits, securities and the like. Five years ago households held only 31% of their wealth in financial assets, as opposed to property. Now the share is about 45%, reckons Goldman Sachs, a bank. The financial system is struggling to put this money to work. Bank loans in yuan grew by only 4.9% in August year-on-year. Loans to households (such as mortgages) fell.

China is also now contending with a less familiar gap in demand (see chart 2). Investment in manufacturing and traditional infrastructure has plunged, according to official figures tracking spending on “fixed” assets (that is, excluding things like stockpiled goods). The numbers are so bleak, they have many analysts scratching their heads. China’s government data often arouse suspicion because they paint a flattering picture. These figures, by contrast, seem too bad to be true.

Other sources also look grim, however. The government’s “general” budget, for example, shows a drop in infrastructure spending in the first half of the year. And money is flowing less quickly into another fiscal pot—government-managed funds, which typically collect proceeds from land sales and plough them into construction. Local governments are meanwhile preoccupied with retiring hidden debt, buying vacant land from struggling property developers and clearing a backlog of arrears to suppliers. This “fiscal crunch” is the prime culprit for the infrastructure slowdown, according to Bank of America.

If this weakness in domestic demand persists, China could easily lapse back into deflation. The worry will become acute if demand for the country’s exports falters, either because of further protectionism or a slowdown in America’s AI-investment boom. Imagining a similar shortfall in demand, John Maynard Keynes in 1942 urged the government to build an ample library of public-works projects that could be speeded up if the rest of the economy weakened and slowed down if it proved strong. These blueprints, he said in a radio address, “can be as ambitious and glorious as the minds of our engineers and architects and social planners can conceive”. The six networks are China’s answer to this same challenge. They provide 25trn-yuan-worth of ambitious blue-prints the central government can implement when necessary to support the economy. “Depending on policymakers’ assessment of how much is needed, they are going to turn the dial a little bit faster or slower,” says Dr Qiao.

In his radio address, Keynes also touched on the “nightmare of finance”. How will all these ambitions be paid for? China’s past infrastructure booms have relied on land sales and the hidden debt raised by off-balance-sheet financing vehicles. That model is no longer feasible or politically tolerable for Beijing. In a moribund housing market, land cannot bring in as much money as it once did. And LGFVs offer less financial wriggle room than they did before. Pan Gongsheng, China’s central-bank governor, has claimed that 70% of them had been shut down or converted into commercial ventures with no local-government guarantees.

The six networks will therefore be financed differently. The money will come from the central government, some of its prominent state-owned enterprises and the “special bonds” it approves for local governments. China’s two big grid companies plan to spend a combined 5trn yuan on power networks over the next half-decade. The three big telecoms operators intend to spend about 260bn yuan between them in just 12 months.

China’s policy banks will also play a prominent role. Their loans are supposed to count as first-loss equity capital for the projects they finance. By bearing some of the risk, these stakes should allow the projects to raise more money—even four or five times more—from commercial banks.

Compared with the last infrastructure boom, the financing should be cheaper. China’s excess saving and unusual lack of “investment hunger” means that interest rates are strikingly low. The central government can now borrow for ten years at less than 1.7%—in an economy that is still growing by about 5% in nominal terms. As the rest of the world contends with inflation and surging bond yields, China is still living in the world of “woke macro”, as some economists have called it. In that world governments felt they could spend their way out of trouble and grow their way out of the resulting debt.

With this financial muscle behind it, China’s ambitious six-networks blueprints should put a floor under its economy. By front-loading the spending, China can be sure to meet its growth target of 4.5-5% for this year. How much it adds to China’s growth over a longer horizon depends on the answers to two nettlesome questions: will the six networks increase productivity? And how much would China have spent on infrastructure anyway?

Sceptics will point out that the “six networks” label is newer than some of the schemes it now names. That is often true of China’s grand projects. The same criticism was levelled at the Belt and Road Initiative, a globe-spanning trade-and-investment plan launched in 2013, and the push for “new productive forces” (high-tech productivity improvements) that Mr Xi began championing a decade later. There is more than a cup or two of old wine in the six new bottles China is now showcasing.

Several analysts have compared the 25trn-yuan spending plans to the money spent in similar categories over the past five years. The vast sum it has allocated to water projects over the next five years (6trn yuan), for example, is similar to the amount spent over the past five. But these calculations also suggest that China could invest about 20% more in the power grid, 3% more in communications and perhaps 300% more in computing capacity.

China’s leaders hope that this new spending will usher in a high-tech productivity miracle. The six networks will, they believe, support a similar number of “emerging pillar” industries: integrated circuits, aerospace, biomedicine, new energy storage, robots and the “low-altitude economy” (which includes drones). They are also keen to cultivate half-a-dozen more speculative “industries of the future”, including quantum technology, nuclear fusion, biomanufacturing, green hydrogen, brain-computer interfaces, embodied intelligence, and 6G mobile-telecoms.

Some of these may be flops. A high failure rate is inevitable in frontier industries. The return on upstream infrastructure may thus be disappointingly low. But as Keynes would no doubt point out: the return on unemployment is even worse.

By alleviating a shortfall in domestic demand, China’s infrastructure push could also improve the country’s global standing. The extra spending will, all else equal, narrow China’s trade surpluses, by raising domestic prices and absorbing exportable goods. That would be good for the global economy. And it might help the cause of rules-based international commerce, which has struggled to cope with such a large, lopsided actor. For all its emphasis on telecoms, computing, electricity and so on, China ultimately owes its prosperity to the larger network of international trade. If the 25trn yuan douses some of the protectionist fires now burning around the world, it will be money well spent.

The leaders of some of China’s trading partners will visit Shenzhen in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit. Perhaps these dignitaries could cross the Pearl river estuary and inspect the Underground Great Wall in Hengqin. If such projects help revive Chinese growth, rebalance the world economy and forestall trade wars, you would have to conclude that these are great pipes.■

item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普会再次会见金正恩吗？

亚洲 | 核不讨论 2026年10月1日 六位美国总统曾试图处理朝鲜的核武器计划，六位都失败了。唐纳德·特朗普想再试一次：他曾表示预计今年将与朝鲜独裁者金正恩会面。计划于11月前往亚洲出席亚太经合组织（APEC）论坛峰会的行程可能提供一个契机；特朗普的前朝鲜特使最近在一次演讲中表示，他甚至可能提议在平壤会面——那里从未有在任美国总统到访过。然而，金正恩已明确表示，只有美国放弃其长期坚持的“无核化”要求（即拆除或移除其政权最强大武器的外交辞令），他才会会面。就在特朗普为重新点燃与金正恩的“兄弟情”而缩减与韩国的长期计划军事演习一个月后，这位朝鲜独裁者在 teenage 女儿的陪同下，监督了一枚新型所谓高超音速导弹的试射。他得意地宣称，这种武器将成为朝鲜敌人的“不治之症”。 金正恩的顽固反映了一种新的自信。数十年来，美国及其盟友，连同中国和俄罗斯，试图施压朝鲜放弃其核武追求。尽管有这些努力，金正恩如今已拥有数十枚核弹头，以及能够将其运至美国本土等遥远目标的导弹。在乌克兰战争中与俄罗斯重新结盟，为金正恩赢得了经济和外交上的喘息空间。对拥核朝鲜的原则性反对正在瓦解。俄罗斯公开接受朝鲜的核地位，其外长称这是一个“已关闭的问题”；中国则对此保持沉默。韩国左翼总统李在明提议将无核化作为一个未来希望实现的目标。特朗普可能会受到诱惑而效仿。如果他这样做，将标志着美国政策的重大转变，对地区安全和全球防扩散努力产生重大影响。朝鲜于1985年签署《不扩散核武器条约》（NPT），同意放弃核武器以换取民用核能援助。但尽管如此，它很快就开始秘密发展核武库。随后数十年间的多轮国际谈判和广泛的经济制裁未能阻止其进展；朝鲜在2006年至2017年间进行了六次核试验。在第一个任期内，特朗普实施了所谓的“极限施压”制裁，用“火与怒”威胁金正恩，然后促成了美朝领导人首次峰会。但在第二次会晤时，谈判在激烈争吵中破裂。此后，美国对朝鲜的影响力已经减弱。过去，经济制裁可能打击平壤政府：在特朗普首个任期的峰会期间，金正恩曾寻求以关闭其主要核设施宁边来换取制裁减免。但近年来，朝鲜因支持弗拉基米尔·普京的乌克兰战争而获得了意外之财。朝鲜向俄罗斯提供了炮弹和弹道导弹，以及约16000名士兵。部分得益于俄罗斯的新支持，朝鲜经济似乎在增长，尽管不均衡。韩国央行估计，2022年至2025年间，朝鲜经济年均增长率达3.4%，相当强劲。朝俄联盟正在深化。9月初，连接两国的第一座公路桥在图们江上开通。俄罗斯去年向朝鲜人发放了超过35000份学生签证；其中许多人被怀疑在俄罗斯工作，包括在为战争制造无人机的工厂里。乌克兰官员担心朝鲜正准备今秋再次部署军队援助俄罗斯。“我们作为平等伙伴合作；我们彼此有想要和需要的东西，”一位俄罗斯学者说。除了食品、燃料和资金，朝鲜主要想要高端技术。韩国官员担心俄罗斯帮助金正恩建造核动力潜艇。俄罗斯的支持也让金正恩得以恢复与中国的关系——中国担心对邻国失去影响力——从而使他对与特朗普重燃“兄弟情”不太感兴趣。自初次会面以来，朝鲜的武器计划也取得了重大进展。过去，朝鲜的核武库尚处于初期阶段，阻止它或许还是可能的。朝鲜于2023年将核地位写入宪法。现在特朗普说朝鲜拥有57枚核弹头；独立估计数字高达120枚（英国拥有225枚）。该政权没有迹象表明会止步于此。据联合国国际原子能机构称，在宁边发现了一座新的铀浓缩设施。韩国总统李在明表示，朝鲜目前每年生产的裂变材料足以制造10至20枚额外弹头。特朗普对伊朗的战争印证了金氏家族将核武器视为终极安全保障的赌注：尽管伊朗接近拥核，但从未跨越核门槛。“尤其是在伊朗战争之后，我相信朝鲜将更倾向于不放弃其核武库，”李在明在6月对《经济学人》表示。因此，要求采取新方法的呼声日益高涨，即将焦点从施压朝鲜放弃核武器转向重启对话，以期减缓其进展。李在明领导的政党倾向于接触政策，他提议采取分阶段方法，首先从冻结朝鲜核计划开始。在美国，风向也在转变。曾在小布什政府期间协助领导对朝谈判的维克多·查认为，美国现在应放弃坚持无核化，转而寻求与朝鲜达成基于军控谈判的“冷和平”。尽管美国官员仍将全面无核化作为表面目标，特朗普已开始随意称朝鲜为“核大国”。即使默认承认朝鲜为核国家，也将为金正恩带来长期寻求的胜利。2016年叛逃的朝鲜高级外交官太永浩表示，金正恩告诉精英们，如果国家坚持下去，美国就会让步并承认朝鲜的核地位，就像它对巴基斯坦所做的那样。与巴基斯坦（或印度）不同，朝鲜签署了《不扩散核武器条约》，并在承诺和平利用的情况下获得了核技术。因此，现在将其核武器合法化可能为未来的扩散者树立一个令人担忧的先例。一项让朝鲜武库完好无损同时让日韩感到暴露的协议，也可能推动美国盟友更接近发展自己的核武器。特朗普在试图解决一个棘手问题的同时，可能冒险制造新的问题。■ 如需获取亚洲政治、经济和安全的独家报道，请订阅我们的每周订阅者专属通讯《亚洲简报》。

Asia

亚洲 | 疏漏与擅断 2026年10月1日 印度的选举工作人员长期以来不畏山地与猛虎，设立投票站——有时仅为一名选民服务。在新德里，一个三人组成的选举委员会以“不让任何选民掉队”为官方座右铭，监督着这一使命。前首席选举专员S.Y.库拉希告诉《经济学人》，如今这届团队正在毁掉这一声誉。这一独立监督机构的资深人士很少公开批评其继任者。抗议者走上街头要求某位专员辞职，则更是罕见。但9月23日《印度快报》刊登两位现任选举专员的爆炸性投诉后，这一切发生了。该报报道称，在他们的首席专员加内什·库马尔领导下，他们认为委员会做出了“未经授权”和“非法”的决定。大规模学生抗议迫使一位教育部长辞职后仅两个月，不...
item.content:encoded:
对偏袒的指控动摇印度选举监督机构

亚洲 | 疏漏与擅断 2026年10月1日

印度的选举工作人员长期以来不畏山地与猛虎，设立投票站——有时仅为一名选民服务。在新德里，一个三人组成的选举委员会以“不让任何选民掉队”为官方座右铭，监督着这一使命。前首席选举专员S.Y.库拉希告诉《经济学人》，如今这届团队正在毁掉这一声誉。这一独立监督机构的资深人士很少公开批评其继任者。抗议者走上街头要求某位专员辞职，则更是罕见。但9月23日《印度快报》刊登两位现任选举专员的爆炸性投诉后，这一切发生了。该报报道称，在他们的首席专员加内什·库马尔领导下，他们认为委员会做出了“未经授权”和“非法”的决定。大规模学生抗议迫使一位教育部长辞职后仅两个月，不当行为的指控再次震动印度政府。抗议者和反对派领导人声称，执政的印度人民党（BJP）已使印度民主的监督机构俯首听命。

据《印度快报》报道，另外两位专员对决策方式提出了内部异议，认为决策未经他们同意就被强行通过。他们抱怨委员会官僚批准了种种障碍，使印度人更难证明自己的投票权。他们还反对将地方工作人员认为合法的数十万选民排除在外。这两位专员拒绝确认相关报道，但也没有否认。“委员会表示自己的决策程序没有问题。

受到特别审查的是一项名称看似平淡无奇的行动。自2025年6月以来，委员会已让印度大部分地区进行选民名册的“特别集中修订”（SIR）；36个邦和中央直辖区中仅有6个尚未启动。迄今为止还算合理：自上次大规模更新以来已过二十年，记录中充斥着死者、重复和过时条目。但这项工程一直混乱不堪——而且往往在各邦选举前仓促推进，没有时间听取异议。由于对证明资格所需文件存在困惑，一些人发现护照和政府自己的数字身份证不足以证明身份，还必须附上离校证书。结果是大规模剥夺选举权。

这项行动可能削减超过1.3亿个名字——其中数千万将是真实选民。情况最糟的是德里，55%的选民要么被删除，要么须在10月29日前说服委员会恢复其资格。在一个地点，729名选民中仅1人得以保留。按照委员会自己的标准，这些数字也颇为异常：其指导方针将超过2%的删除率归类为“可疑”。委员会承诺将重新审视这一过程，但许多政治分析人士称SIR是印度几十年来最大的选举丑闻。

穆斯林尤其容易面临被删除的风险。在印度各地，地方人民党人物带着成摞表格出现，推动选举工作人员成批删除选民。在人民党渴望数十年并于5月赢下的西孟加拉邦，偏袒的指控最为激烈。那里超过11%的名字消失了。在340万提出申诉的孟加拉人中，在选举日前得到听证的不到0.05%。在申诉过程中，法庭发现90%的申诉人自始至终都是有效选民。

一个显而易见的问题是SIR能否左右选举结果。相关证据尚不明朗。在西孟加拉邦，仅反现任情绪可能就足以让人民党获胜，但删除人数多的选区也持续向该党倾斜。人民党最激烈的地区对手——泰米尔纳德邦首席部长M.K.斯大林和西孟加拉邦首席部长玛玛塔·班纳吉——各自以小于被删除选民数量的差距输掉了自己的席位。

在印度，各种色彩的政党长期以来都与选民欺诈有染。不同之处在于，过去选举委员会一直是制止其搞鬼的相当坚定的制约力量。但在2023年，人民党无视最高法院命令，通过了一项法律，实际上让政府得以安插其提名人选。这使人们对库马尔先生的公正性产生怀疑，因为他正是在新规则下获任的。反对派领导人和街头抗议者呼吁将他免职甚至起诉。主要反对党国大党的议会领袖拉胡尔·甘地希望以叛国罪审判他。■

订阅我们的免费周报《要闻印度》，持续关注我们对印度的报道。

item.title: Vietnam's high-tech dreams come with an electricity problem
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Powerless Oct 1st 2026 TO MANY PEOPLE Vietnam’s promotion in July to “upper middle-income” status by the World Bank vindicated almost 40 years of doi moi or “renovation,” the country’s period of economic opening. To Lam, the chairman of Vietnam’s Communist Party, is not satisfied: “If we ...
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam's high-tech dreams come with an electricity problem

Asia | Powerless

Oct 1st 2026

TO MANY PEOPLE Vietnam’s promotion in July to “upper middle-income” status by the World Bank vindicated almost 40 years of doi moi or “renovation,” the country’s period of economic opening. To Lam, the chairman of Vietnam’s Communist Party, is not satisfied: “If we continue with old methods, we may achieve temporary growth,” he warned in May, “but it will be difficult to create sustainable growth …or escape the middle-income trap.”

Wages for Vietnamese workers are rising, which threatens to squeeze already narrow margins in the manufacturing sector. So before its workforce is priced out, Vietnam’s government hopes to leap up the value chain. It intends to manufacture high-tech products like semiconductors, which it currently merely assembles with comparatively little value added. But chipmaking takes lots of energy. And Vietnam, which has only recently conquered chronic blackouts, needs reforms to match its ambition. Luckily, it has a plan. Vietnam aims to bring liquefied natural gas, or LNG, into the power mix. Imported gas can provide an efficient, steady stream of power and is ideal for energy-intensive industrial parks. By 2030, Vietnam hopes to generate about 10% of its electricity from the stuff.

But it won’t meet that goal. VinGroup, the country’s largest conglomerate, ended a $6.7bn LNG power-plant project in March, citing high costs. The construction of new LNG power plants is stalling across the country, and the handful that are moving forward are mostly run by state-owned enterprises, including Vietnam Electricity (EVN). So far, LNG contributes only about 1.6% of Vietnam’s electricity.

Vietnam is not entirely to blame. The Iran war has hit Asia-bound LNG hard; import prices have risen by 146% since the end of February. At current prices, importing LNG at the rates envisioned by the 2030 plan would cost “$14bn–18bn a year—equivalent to 16–20% of the country’s foreign-exchange reserves, every year,” says Phillip Solomon of BRG, a consultancy. But this pressure will fade if and when global prices recede.

The bigger problem is political. Electricity in Vietnam is highly subsidised. State-owned producers are told by the government to sell their power at an artificially low cost, which makes it easier to enforce aggressive price caps. LNG does not work that way. Building a large fleet of LNG power plants takes huge amounts of capital and expertise that are beyond the state’s ability to provide. Only foreign operators can do the trick, and they typically will demand higher rates than the government prefers to pay. This puts Vietnam in a bind. It can either pay for LNG, which makes power subsidies more expensive to maintain, or abandon gas imports, jeopardising its high-tech hopes.

Vietnam has struggled with this choice before. Back in 2017 it was able to attract foreign companies for solar projects with a generous feed-in-tariff, a baseline rate that the state pays for power. But these rates were too expensive to maintain, so EVN retroactively cut them in 2025, slashing returns for investments totalling about $13bn. As a result, many foreign power developers already think twice before doing business in Vietnam. ■

item.title: Japan’s tea farmers enjoy a matcha boom
item.description:
Asia

Asia | The green tea wars Oct 1st 2026 ATOP A HILL in Kagoshima, on Japan’s southern island of Kyushu, neat rows of green tea bushes stretch across a vast field. When Nishi Toshimi inherited his family farm two decades ago, the industry was heading downhill; prices were falling and sales shrinki...
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s tea farmers enjoy a matcha boom

Asia | The green tea wars

Oct 1st 2026

ATOP A HILL in Kagoshima, on Japan’s southern island of Kyushu, neat rows of green tea bushes stretch across a vast field. When Nishi Toshimi inherited his family farm two decades ago, the industry was heading downhill; prices were falling and sales shrinking. Then the world went crazy for matcha. The boom of the past few years has felt “like a miracle,” he says.

Japan’s green-tea exports reached 12,600 tonnes last year, three times as much as a decade earlier; prices have also surged. Unlike Kyoto, famed for its coveted Uji matcha, or Shizuoka, a traditional producer of brewed green tea, Kagoshima is barely a household name. Yet the matcha boom has transformed its fortunes. In 2024 it became Japan’s top tea producer for the first time and now grows around 40% of its tencha, the leaf that is ground to make matcha powder. Even so, Japan is struggling to keep up with global demand. Its tea industry is in surprisingly poor shape, beset by ageing farmers, labour shortages and competition from China.

While the world craves matcha, most Japanese drink sencha, made by brewing tea leaves in the normal way, rather than dissolving matcha powder. Yet demand at home has long been falling as habits have changed. Consumption of tea leaves fell from 527 grams per person in 1970 to 233 in 2024. Farmers have left the business or retired without successors; between 2005 and 2025 the area devoted to tea cultivation shrank by 31%.

Nor can all farmers lean into the matcha boom. Producing tencha requires different cultivation methods, including shading bushes before harvest, and costly processing facilities.

Many in the industry think that Japan’s future lies at the high end. China, which produces 70% of the world’s matcha, may dwarf it in quantity, but Japanese producers argue that their matcha is tastier and far more sophisticated. Tea came to Japan from China, but Japan developed its own traditions around it, most famously the tea ceremony. Mr Nishi thinks Japan should establish itself as the Champagne region of matcha. “Otherwise, we’re going to lose out”, he says.■

item.content:encoded:
科莫多游客激增带来新危险

亚洲 | 游客与龙 2026年10月1日 它曾挺过冰河时代、干旱和飓风，但科莫多巨蜥能否挺过大众旅游的冲击，尚不得而知。近年来，科莫多岛及其补给基地——位于附近更大的弗洛勒斯岛上的纳闽巴焦——一直是印度尼西亚推动旅游业扩张的风口浪尖。两年前卸任的印尼总统佐科·维多多曾表示，他想打造“十个新巴厘岛”，旨在为本国带来更多就业机会和高收入。巴厘岛长期以来一直是印尼的头号旅游目的地，带来大量外汇，为巴厘岛居民和来自全国各地的务工人员提供就业机会。维多多先生的重点名单上赫然列着纳闽巴焦，以及更远处的科莫多国家公园。毕竟，这里拥有一项独特的旅游吸引物——科莫多巨蜥，一种可长到十英尺（三米）长、重达80公斤的巨型蜥蜴，仅存于科莫多岛及附近几个较小岛屿上。据估计，仅有约1300只成年“陆上鳄鱼”（印尼一些人对它们的称呼）幸存。从经济上看，这一计划已经奏效。纳闽巴焦如今挤满了潜水店、餐馆、酒店和咖啡店。其港口每天将成船热情的游客送往科莫多岛（该岛没有自己的机场，只能乘船抵达）及其周边水域和岛屿。但去年12月，该公园及其游客遭遇了一次严重冲击。四名西班牙游客——包括瓦伦西亚足球俱乐部教练费尔南多·马丁及其三名子女——在乘船游览时因船只在大浪中沉没而遇难。这一事件迫使公园暂时关闭。纳闽巴焦弗洛勒斯旅游局（为落实前总统构想而设立的机构）市场经理西西莉亚·莱尼塔·杰马纳表示，维多多的计划过于成功了。该地区正苦于应对惊人的增长。2025年，该地区接待游客超过50万人次，同比增长21%。十年间游客数量增长了五倍。杰马纳女士说，她的机构长期以来一直敦促海事当局和国家公园管理局限制进入，尤其是在危险的雨季。12月的死亡事件引发了广泛的震惊。“如果天气条件不利，就不应批准出航，”杰马纳女士说。她的机构一直在寻找其他可推广的旅游景点，例如与16世纪定居该岛的葡萄牙商人和传教士相关的遗址，以及大约20年前在那里发现的弗洛勒斯人——已灭绝的“霍比特人”这一现代人类近亲——遗骸相关的地点。弗洛勒斯岛还有其他的国家公园和活火山。但归根结底，游客还是想看巨蜥。不幸的是，许多游客到了那里并不知道该如何表现。有些人靠得太近——这种动物可能懒洋洋地躺着，但也可能具有攻击性，并且有过袭击人类的记录。它还有一口致命的有毒咬伤。今年早些时候，科莫多实施了每日1000名游客的初步上限。运气好的话，巨蜥们会得到安抚。■ 如需获取亚洲政治、经济和安全方面的独家报道，请订阅我们的每周订户专属通讯《亚洲简报》。
